examples.label: present
examples.text:
Sugar practical
The pear juice goes into a small test tube. Add Benedict's reagent and place the tube in a hot water bath. Heat it and inspect for a coloured precipitate: green through orange to brick red indicates reducing sugar. A sample that remains blue after this procedure is negative. Compare it with water treated in the same way.

examples.label: partial
examples.text: Warm the food sample with Benedict solution in a water bath. This is a test for reducing sugar. A blue solution after heating means a positive result; a brick-red deposit means no reducing sugar was present. The colour observations should be written down before disposing of the contents.

examples.label: missing
examples.text:
Carbohydrates
Glucose and fructose are simple sugars. Starch consists of many sugar units and occurs in cereal grains. Sucrose is a disaccharide. These classes differ in their structures and some of their properties. Benedict's test is the title of the next page; no laboratory instructions are recorded here.

examples.label: present
examples.text: The test wire was kept at the same temperature. At 1.5 V it carried 0.3 A, and at 3 V it carried 0.6 A. The ratio V/I stays 5 ohms: current and potential difference are directly proportional. This is Ohm's law, V = IR, with physical conditions held constant.

examples.label: partial
examples.text: Ohm's law: potential difference is directly proportional to current. Resistance equals their ratio, R = V/I, and V = IR. A resistor carrying 2 A at 10 V has resistance 5 ohms. This relationship is true for every component at every temperature, even when a filament becomes much hotter.

examples.label: missing
examples.text:
Electrical safety
A fuse melts if too much current flows. The earth wire provides a path that can help protective devices disconnect a faulty appliance. Dry insulation around a wire reduces the chance of contact with live metal. Turn off the supply before replacing a fuse.

examples.label: present
examples.text: Oxygen-16 and oxygen-18 are isotopes. Each nucleus contains eight protons. The first has eight neutrons and the second ten. Isotopes therefore have the same proton number but different neutron counts, giving different mass numbers while remaining the same element.

examples.label: partial
examples.text: Boron-10 and boron-11 are called isotopes. Their mass numbers are different. The boron-10 nucleus has five protons and five neutrons, while boron-11 has six protons and five neutrons. They remain the same element despite having different numbers of protons.

examples.label: missing
examples.text:
Atoms in chemical bonds
Sodium transfers its outer electron to chlorine. Sodium becomes positively charged and chlorine becomes negatively charged. Opposite charges attract, forming an ionic lattice. This rearranges electrons; it does not change either nucleus during the reaction.

examples.label: present
examples.text:
Comparison
Sexual reproduction: male and female gametes unite during fertilisation to form a zygote.
Asexual reproduction: a single parent produces new organisms without the union of gametes; a potato tuber producing new plants is an example. The new plants are usually genetically alike to the parent, whereas sexual offspring can show inherited variation.

examples.label: partial
examples.text: During fertilisation the sperm and egg gametes fuse to form a zygote. The zygote divides and develops into a new organism. This is sexual reproduction. In a flowering plant the male gamete reaches the ovule through a pollen tube. No second reproductive method is described on this page.

examples.label: missing
examples.text:
Seed structure
The seed coat protects the embryo. The plumule develops into the shoot and the radicle into the root. Cotyledons may contain stored food. Soaking a bean softens its outer coat and makes these structures easier to observe under a hand lens.

examples.label: present
examples.text:
--- Page 1 ---
Combination joins substances to form a single product, for example carbon burning to carbon dioxide. Decomposition breaks a compound into simpler products, for example water decomposing into hydrogen and oxygen.
--- Page 2 ---
In single displacement an element replaces another in a compound, such as iron replacing copper in copper sulphate. In double displacement two compounds exchange ions, as when barium chloride and sodium sulphate produce barium sulphate and sodium chloride.

examples.label: partial
examples.text:
Combination and decomposition
Two or more reactants form a single product in combination. One compound breaks into simpler substances in decomposition. Hydrogen and oxygen making water illustrates the first pattern, while heated silver oxide giving silver and oxygen illustrates the second. Displacement reactions are listed as homework but not explained in these notes.

examples.label: missing
examples.text:
Conservation of mass
In a closed system, total mass before a reaction equals total mass afterwards. Gas can escape from an open vessel and make the measured mass appear to decrease. Using a sealed vessel helps account for every product. The balance measures the whole apparatus before and after the change.

examples.label: present
examples.text:
Quiet breathing
Breathing in: diaphragm contracts and moves down; ribs lift up and out through intercostal muscle contraction. Chest volume becomes larger, pressure falls, air flows into the lungs.
Breathing out: these muscles relax, the diaphragm returns to a dome and ribs move down and in. Smaller chest volume raises pressure, sending air out. The pressure is compared with atmospheric pressure in each phase.

examples.label: partial
examples.text: Expiration occurs as the diaphragm and intercostal muscles relax. The diaphragm becomes dome-shaped and the ribs move down and in. Chest volume decreases, pressure rises and air moves out of the lungs. This revision card only describes quiet expiration.

examples.label: missing
examples.text:
Cellular respiration
Cells break down glucose to release usable energy. With oxygen, carbon dioxide and water are formed. The energy supports processes such as muscle activity and active transport. Respiration happens in living cells and is distinct from simply moving air along an airway.

examples.label: present
examples.text:
Doped silicon
A very small controlled amount of impurity is added to increase conductivity. A pentavalent donor supplies an extra electron, producing n-type material with electrons as majority carriers. A trivalent acceptor creates an electron vacancy or hole, producing p-type material with holes as majority carriers. The letters indicate the dominant carriers, not a net charge on the whole crystal.

examples.label: partial
examples.text: Doping introduces a controlled impurity into a pure semiconductor. Pentavalent donors make n-type material, but holes are its majority carriers. Trivalent acceptors make p-type material, whose majority carriers are electrons. The five-valence and three-valence impurities distinguish the two types.

examples.label: missing
examples.text:
Metals and insulators
In a metal some electrons can move through the structure and carry current. Plastic covering around a cable has very few mobile charge carriers under ordinary conditions. The copper core conducts while the covering insulates. The choice of materials suits their different jobs.

examples.label: present
examples.text: A 0.25 kg sample has specific heat 800 J per kilogram per degree. Its temperature changes from 12 C to 22 C, a rise of 10 C. Q = mc times the change = 0.25 x 800 x 10 = 2000 J. No change of state occurs. For insulated mixing, the hotter body's heat loss equals the cooler body's heat gain until both reach a common final temperature.

examples.label: partial
examples.text: A 0.25 kg sample with specific heat 800 J per kilogram per degree warms from 12 C to 22 C. Using Q = mc times the temperature change, Q = 0.25 x 800 x 10 = 20000 J. The mass is in kg and the answer in joules. In an insulated mixture, heat lost equals heat gained.

examples.label: missing
examples.text:
Thermal expansion
A metal rod becomes longer when heated because the average spacing between particles increases. Bridges have expansion gaps to accommodate changes in length. Liquid expansion is used in some thermometers. The particles themselves do not become larger in this account.

examples.label: present
examples.text:
Separating leaf colours
Put a small pigment spot on a pencil baseline and let it dry. Suspend the paper with the spot above the liquid solvent surface. Paper is the stationary phase; moving solvent is the mobile phase. Pigments have different attractions to paper and solvent, so they travel different distances and separate into bands. Mark the solvent front before the paper dries.

examples.label: partial
examples.text: For paper chromatography keep the starting sample spot above the solvent level. Paper remains stationary and solvent moves through it. All dyes have exactly the same attraction to paper and solvent and move at the same speed. Their different colours alone cause separate bands to appear at different heights.

examples.label: missing
examples.text:
Recovering salt
Warm a salt solution gently so some water evaporates. Allow the concentrated solution to cool, and crystals form. Separate and dry the crystals. The dissolved salt is recovered by crystallisation; no moving solvent front or paper strip is used.

examples.label: present
examples.text: A heater takes 2.5 A at 200 V. P = VI = 200 x 2.5 = 500 W = 0.5 kW. Power is electrical energy transferred per second; 500 W means 500 joules each second. Total energy used depends on the operating time as well as this power.

examples.label: partial
examples.text: P = VI gives electrical power from voltage and current. A 200 V appliance drawing 2.5 A uses 500 W, meaning 500 joules per second. Power is a rate of energy transfer. To change units, 500 W = 5 kW; divide watts by 100 to obtain kilowatts.

examples.label: missing
examples.text:
Electrical energy transformations
A rechargeable battery stores energy chemically. When it powers a torch, chemical energy is transferred electrically and eventually becomes light and heat. Recharging transfers energy back into the battery. An energy-flow diagram represents these changes with arrows.
